# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## The Consensus Trap

There is a quiet ritual that plays out in conference rooms every day. A discussion winds down, someone looks around the table and asks, "So are we all aligned?" Heads nod. Someone types up notes that say the group "agreed to move forward." The meeting ends on time, everyone feels productive, and the decision is recorded as settled.

Then, weeks later, nothing happens. Or worse, something happens—half-heartedly, in three different directions, with key people quietly doing the opposite of what was "agreed." The consensus, it turns out, was an illusion. It was not agreement but a kind of mutual truce: everyone was tired, no one wanted to be the difficult one, and the path of least resistance was to nod along.

We tend to treat unanimity as the sign of a successful meeting. But agreement can be a mask. It can hide the fact that people understand the same words to mean different things, or that they hold private doubts they never voiced, or that the group simply hasn't thought hard enough to discover what it actually disagrees about.
